title: Palazzo Vecchio in Florence: the museum, the Arnolfo Tower or both, and what each ticket covers
subtitle: One building, two visits that are ticketed apart, a courtyard that is free, and a church of statues two minutes away.
excerpt: What you see in the museum of Palazzo Vecchio, what the climb of the Arnolfo Tower adds, which parts are free, what the three partner listings include, and why Orsanmichele round the corner deserves half an hour.

meta_title: Palazzo Vecchio: museum, Arnolfo Tower, which ticket
meta_description: The museum of Palazzo Vecchio and the Arnolfo Tower are ticketed apart. What each shows, what is free, what the tickets cover, and Orsanmichele nearby.

featured_image.alt: The entrance of Palazzo Vecchio in Florence, with the copy of the David and the statue of Hercules and Cacus on either side of the door

content_html:
[place attraction="palazzo-vecchio" city="florence"]

In 1299 the republic of Florence began a fortress for its own government. The priors, the guildsmen who ran the city for two months at a time, lived inside it for their whole term and were not allowed out. The tower above them, about 94 metres high, stands off-centre because it was built on top of an older family tower that the builders kept.

Near the top of that tower is a small cell. Cosimo de' Medici the Elder was locked in it in 1433, before his enemies settled for exile. The friar Girolamo Savonarola waited in it in 1498, before he was hanged and burned on the square below. In 1540 Cosimo's descendant, Duke Cosimo I, moved his court into the building, and a few years later moved it out again, across the river to the Pitti Palace. The palace he left became the old one: Palazzo Vecchio. It is still the town hall of Florence, and it is visited in parts that are ticketed apart.

What is free

You can walk through the main door without a ticket. The first courtyard, redesigned by Michelozzo in the fifteenth century and painted for a Medici wedding in 1565, is open to everybody, with a copy of Verrocchio's little bronze boy holding a dolphin on its fountain.

Outside, the square is a sculpture gallery. The David by the door is a copy placed there in 1910: the original went to the Accademia in 1873. Beside it stands Bandinelli's Hercules and Cacus. Under the arches of the Loggia dei Lanzi are Cellini's bronze Perseus of 1554 and Giambologna's Rape of the Sabines, both originals, both free.

The museum

The museum is the palace itself. Allow an hour and a half.

  • The Hall of the Five Hundred. Built in the 1490s for the great council of Savonarola's republic, 54 metres long. Leonardo and Michelangelo were each hired to paint a battle on its walls, and neither finished. What you see is the work of Giorgio Vasari, who raised the roof for Cosimo I and covered walls and ceiling with Medici victories. Michelangelo's marble Victory stands against one wall.
  • The Studiolo of Francesco I. A small windowless room of painted cupboards off the great hall, made in the 1570s for a duke who preferred alchemy to government. It is usually seen from the doorway.
  • The apartments upstairs. The rooms of the Elements, the apartment of Eleonora of Toledo with a chapel painted by Bronzino, and a balcony that looks down into the great hall.
  • The Hall of the Lilies, with Donatello's bronze Judith and Holofernes, the original.
  • The Hall of Maps. Fifty-three maps of the world as it was known in the 1560s, painted on the doors of cupboards around a large globe.

The Hall of the Five Hundred, with the ceiling and the battle scenes of Giorgio Vasari. Photo: Gary Campbell-Hall, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0.

The Hall of Maps: the known world of the 1560s, painted on cupboard doors. Photo: Zairon, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 4.0.

The Arnolfo Tower

The tower is a separate visit with a separate ticket. You climb a narrow stone stair, more than two hundred steps with no lift, past the cell and up to the gallery under the bells. The view is the one the cathedral dome cannot give you: the dome itself, close and level, with the whole city around it.

Three things to know. The number of people allowed up at one time is small, so entry is by time slot. The tower closes when it rains. And young children are not admitted: the partner's listing gives a minimum age of six, and says under-18s must come with an adult.

The cathedral from the top of the Arnolfo Tower. Photo: Manuelarosi, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

Which to choose

  • One hour, and you like rooms and stories: the museum.
  • You want the view and do not mind stairs: the tower. It is a shorter climb than the cathedral dome, and easier to book.
  • Half a day: both. The tower first, while your legs are fresh, then the rooms.
  • Rain forecast: the museum only. A tower ticket is of no use on a wet day.

What the partner's listings include

  • Palazzo Vecchio, Arnolfo Tower, Museum: entry ticket and audio guide. Both visits. The time you choose is for the tower, which comes first, and the listing says you go into the palace an hour later. An identity document is asked for when you collect the audio guide.
  • Palazzo Vecchio and Museum: entry ticket with optional video or audio guide. The museum only. The description talks about climbing the tower, but the list of what is not included names it: "Admission to Arnolfo Tower". Trust the list.
  • The Palazzo Vecchio audio tour. Commentary in the partner's app on your own phone, and no ticket. You buy entry at the desk. Bring earphones.
  • Orsanmichele Church and Museum. A plain entry ticket for the building described below, without a guide.

These are the tickets and the audio tour our partner sells for Palazzo Vecchio and Orsanmichele, with today's prices:

[partner city="florence" match="palazzo,vecchio,orsanmichele" limit="4"]

Orsanmichele, round the corner

Two minutes north of the square, on the street that leads to the cathedral, stands a tall square block that looks like neither a church nor a palace. It was built from 1337 as the city's grain market, an open hall with storerooms above. A painting of the Virgin on one of its pillars drew so many pilgrims that the arches were walled in and the market hall became a church. The grain stayed upstairs. You can still see the openings of the chutes in the pillars.

The guilds of Florence each had a niche on the outside walls and filled it with a statue of their patron saint. Ghiberti cast a bronze John the Baptist for the cloth merchants. Donatello carved Saint Mark for the linen weavers and Saint George for the armourers. Verrocchio made Christ and the doubting Thomas for the merchants' court. The figures in the niches today are copies. Most of the originals stand together upstairs, in the museum, and the Saint George is in the Bargello.

Inside the church, look for the marble tabernacle by Orcagna, finished in 1359, built around Bernardo Daddi's Madonna. Orsanmichele belongs to the state museums of the Bargello and not to the city, so a Palazzo Vecchio ticket does not cover it. It reopened after restoration in 2024 and has been visited with a ticket since. Half an hour is enough.

Orsanmichele: the arches of the old grain market, walled in, and one of the guild niches. Photo: Zairon, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 4.0.

Practical

The palace has long closed early one day a week, traditionally on Thursday afternoon, and rooms can shut without much notice for city ceremonies. The Hall of the Five Hundred is still used for them. Current hours are on our pages for Palazzo Vecchio and Orsanmichele.

From here

The Uffizi begins at the corner of the palace and the Ponte Vecchio is five minutes away. In the other direction, the street past Orsanmichele brings you to the cathedral in another five. See what else there is in Florence, or open the trip planner for Italy.

Cover photo: Andrzej Otrębski, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

faqs.q: Is the Arnolfo Tower included in the Palazzo Vecchio ticket?
faqs.a: Not in the museum ticket. The tower is a separate visit with its own ticket and time slot, and there are combined tickets that name both.

faqs.q: Is the Palazzo Vecchio tower worth it?
faqs.a: Yes, for the close view of the cathedral dome and the roofs of Florence. It means more than two hundred steps with no lift, and it closes when it rains.

faqs.q: How long do you need at Palazzo Vecchio?
faqs.a: About an hour and a half for the museum, and another forty-five minutes if you climb the tower.

faqs.q: Can you visit Palazzo Vecchio for free?
faqs.a: The first courtyard is open without a ticket, and so are the statues on the square and in the Loggia dei Lanzi. The museum rooms and the tower need tickets.

faqs.q: What is inside Orsanmichele?
faqs.a: A church in a former grain market, with Orcagna's marble tabernacle, and a museum upstairs holding the original guild statues by Ghiberti, Donatello and Verrocchio.

title: Rome when the Vatican and the Colosseum are sold out: five quieter museums and how to choose
subtitle: Greek marbles, a private palace, the Etruscans, the story of the city and a Baroque gallery, none of which needs booking weeks ahead.
excerpt: Palazzo Altemps, Palazzo Doria Pamphilj, Villa Giulia, the Museum of Rome and Palazzo Barberini: what each one shows, who it suits, how long it takes, and what the partner tickets for them really include.
focus_keyword: Rome museums when the Vatican is sold out
longtail_phrases: what to do in Rome if the Vatican Museums are sold out
is Palazzo Doria Pamphilj worth visiting
is Palazzo Altemps worth it
which museums in Rome are not crowded
is Villa Giulia worth visiting
meta_title: Rome's quieter museums when the Vatican is sold out
meta_description: Five museums in Rome that rarely sell out: Altemps, Doria Pamphilj, Villa Giulia, the Museum of Rome, Barberini. What each shows and what tickets include.

featured_image.alt: The courtyard of Palazzo Altemps in Rome, with two storeys of arcades and antique statues under the arches

content_html:
[place attraction="palazzo-altemps" city="rome"]

In 1621 a new pope, Gregory XV, made his nephew Ludovico Ludovisi a cardinal at the age of twenty-five. The pope lived only two more years, and the nephew used them well. He laid out a villa on the Pincian hill and filled it with ancient sculpture, bought from older collections and dug out of his own grounds, which lay over the gardens of imperial Rome.

The villa lasted until the 1880s, when the family sold the land for building. The streets around Via Veneto stand on it now. During the works, in 1887, a marble relief of a goddess rising from the sea came out of the ground. The state bought the Ludovisi sculptures in 1901, and since 1997 they have stood in a palace near Piazza Navona that most visitors walk past. It is one of several museums in Rome where you can decide to go on the same morning, which you cannot say of the Vatican or the Colosseum.

Palazzo Altemps: Greek and Roman sculpture

A Renaissance palace bought in 1568 by Cardinal Marco Sittico Altemps, with a painted loggia and a private church. The sculptures are shown a few to a room, as a collector would have placed them. Look for the Ludovisi Throne, the relief found in 1887; the Gaul who kills himself beside his dying wife; the seated Ares; and a huge battle sarcophagus of the third century. Allow an hour and a half.

Altemps is one seat of the National Roman Museum. The others include Palazzo Massimo, near Termini station, with the painted garden room from the villa of Livia, and the Baths of Diocletian.

The Ludovisi Throne in Palazzo Altemps, found in Rome in 1887. Photo: Marie-Lan Nguyen, via Wikimedia Commons.

Palazzo Doria Pamphilj: a family's paintings, still at home

The palace on Via del Corso is private, and the family still lives in part of it. The gallery runs round a courtyard in four wings, hung frame to frame as in the eighteenth century, with a Gallery of Mirrors along one side. The picture people come for is Velázquez's portrait of the Pamphilj pope, Innocent X, painted in 1650, kept in a small room of its own beside Bernini's bust of the same man. There are also two early Caravaggios, the Rest on the Flight into Egypt and the Penitent Magdalene. Allow an hour and a half. Because it is private, state passes and free days do not apply.

The Gallery of Mirrors in Palazzo Doria Pamphilj. Photo: Sailko, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 3.0.

Villa Giulia: the Etruscans

Pope Julius III built this villa outside the walls in the early 1550s, with Vignola, Ammannati and Vasari among his architects, as a place to spend the day. Since 1889 it has been the national museum of the Etruscans, the people who ruled central Italy before Rome. Its best-known piece is the Sarcophagus of the Spouses, a terracotta couple reclining at a banquet, made in Cerveteri in the sixth century BC. The Apollo of Veii and the gold tablets from Pyrgi are here too. Allow two hours. The villa lies north of the Borghese gardens, a tram ride or a twenty-minute walk from Piazza del Popolo, and it has been closed on Mondays.

The Sarcophagus of the Spouses, made in Cerveteri in the sixth century BC, in Villa Giulia. Photo: Sailko, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

The Museum of Rome in Palazzo Braschi

At the southern end of Piazza Navona, in the last palace built in Rome for a pope's family: it was begun in the 1790s for a nephew of Pius VI. The museum tells the story of the city from the Middle Ages to the nineteenth century, through paintings of festivals and processions, views of streets that no longer exist, portraits and furniture. The staircase, with its columns of red granite, is a sight in itself, and the upper windows look straight down on the piazza. An hour is enough.

Palazzo Barberini: Raphael, Caravaggio and a ceiling

Begun in 1627 for the family of Urban VIII, by three architects in turn: Maderno, Bernini and Borromini. Bernini built the square staircase and Borromini the oval one. The great hall has Pietro da Cortona's ceiling, painted in the 1630s to glorify the Barberini. On the walls of the gallery are Raphael's Fornarina, Caravaggio's Judith Beheading Holofernes and Holbein's portrait of Henry VIII. The ticket has also covered the Galleria Corsini, a smaller collection across the river in Trastevere. Allow two hours.

Palazzo Barberini, begun in 1627 for the family of Pope Urban VIII. Photo: Mallowtek, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.

Which one for whom

  • You wanted the Vatican for its ancient sculpture: Palazzo Altemps.
  • You wanted paintings: Palazzo Barberini, or Doria Pamphilj for a private palace that feels lived in.
  • You wanted ancient history and the Colosseum is full: Villa Giulia, for the people who came before the Romans.
  • You have an hour around Piazza Navona: the Museum of Rome or Altemps. Both are within three minutes of the fountains.
  • It is Monday: the state museums are usually closed, and Doria Pamphilj has been open.

Reading the partner's tickets

Several of these are sold through a local agency, which changes how you get in.

  • Palazzo Altemps: reserved entry. The listing names three sites: Altemps, Palazzo Massimo and the Baths of Diocletian. You do not go to the museum door first. You exchange a voucher at the agency's office on Piazza Navona, where a short video is shown.
  • Museum of Rome: reserved entry. Entry to Palazzo Braschi, with the same exchange at the same office. Exhibitions are not included.
  • Palazzo Doria Pamphilj. Entry to the gallery. The listing excludes the gallery's own audio guide and the private apartments.
  • Villa Giulia. Entry, shown at the door.
  • Largo Argentina. Entry to the sunken square of four temples where Julius Caesar was killed, opened to visitors on walkways in 2023. The voucher is exchanged at an office near Piazza Venezia.
  • Palazzo Venezia. A bundle: the palace museum, the lift to the terrace of the Victor Emmanuel monument and the Risorgimento museum.

The audio guide named in most of these is a general app about the city, not commentary on the rooms. Palazzo Barberini is sold by the same partner as a plain ticket for both galleries, but it is filed under a different list, so look for it on our Rome page.

These are the tickets our partner sells for the quieter museums of central Rome, with today's prices:

[partner city="vatican-city" match="giulia,pamphilj,altemps,reserved,argentina" limit="6"]

Practical

State museums in Italy have been free on the first Sunday of the month, which is the one day these rooms fill. Bags larger than a handbag go to the cloakroom. Hours are on our pages for Palazzo Altemps, the Galleria Doria Pamphilj, Villa Giulia and Palazzo Barberini.

From here

Altemps and the Museum of Rome leave you on Piazza Navona, five minutes from the Pantheon. From Doria Pamphilj the Trevi Fountain is a short walk east. From Villa Giulia you can walk back through the Borghese gardens to the Spanish Steps. Open the trip planner for Italy to fit them into your days.

Cover photo: JTSH26, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

faqs.q: What can you do in Rome if the Vatican Museums are sold out?
faqs.a: Go to a museum that rarely sells out: Palazzo Altemps for ancient sculpture, Palazzo Barberini or Doria Pamphilj for paintings, Villa Giulia for the Etruscans.

faqs.q: Is Palazzo Doria Pamphilj worth visiting?
faqs.a: Yes. It is a private palace hung as in the eighteenth century, with Velázquez's portrait of Innocent X and two early Caravaggios. Allow an hour and a half.

faqs.q: Is Palazzo Altemps worth it?
faqs.a: Yes, if you like ancient sculpture. The Ludovisi collection is shown a few pieces to a room in a Renaissance palace beside Piazza Navona, usually without crowds.

faqs.q: Which museums in Rome are not crowded?
faqs.a: Palazzo Altemps, Villa Giulia, the Museum of Rome in Palazzo Braschi, Palazzo Barberini and the Galleria Doria Pamphilj are all quiet on most days.

faqs.q: Is Villa Giulia worth visiting?
faqs.a: Yes, for the Etruscans: the Sarcophagus of the Spouses, the Apollo of Veii and the gold tablets from Pyrgi, in a villa built for a pope in the 1550s. It takes about two hours.

title: Ostia Antica or Tivoli: a half-day trip from Rome by train or bus, and which one to choose
subtitle: A Roman port town half an hour away on a city ticket, or a hill town with two villas and a waterfall: what fits into half a day and what does not.
excerpt: How to reach Ostia Antica and Tivoli without a car, what you see at Ostia, how Villa d'Este, Hadrian's Villa and Villa Gregoriana differ, where Castel Gandolfo fits, and what the partner tickets include.
focus_keyword: Ostia Antica or Tivoli from Rome
secondary_keywords: Ostia Antica by train from Rome
longtail_phrases: how to get to Ostia Antica from Rome
is Ostia Antica worth visiting
can you see Villa d'Este and Hadrian's Villa in one day
how to get to Tivoli from Rome by train
is Ostia Antica better than Pompeii
meta_title: Ostia Antica or Tivoli: half-day trip from Rome
meta_description: Ostia Antica by train on a city ticket, or Tivoli for Villa d'Este, Hadrian's Villa and Villa Gregoriana: what fits in half a day and what tickets cover.

featured_image.alt: The stone seats of the Roman theatre at Ostia Antica, with umbrella pines behind them under a clear sky

content_html:
[place attraction="ostia-antica" city="rome"]

Ostia was where Rome met the sea. Its name comes from the Latin for a river mouth, and for centuries the grain that fed the capital was unloaded here, stored, taxed and sent up the Tiber on barges. At its height the town held tens of thousands of people: dockers, shippers, bakers, innkeepers and the clerks of trading firms from every coast of the Mediterranean.

Then the river let it down. Silt pushed the shore outwards until the sea was three kilometres away. New harbours to the north took the trade, malaria took the people, and by the early Middle Ages Ostia was empty. Sand and river mud covered it and kept it. What was dug out is a whole Roman town, half an hour from the centre of Rome, and on most days nearly empty. The other classic half day from the city is Tivoli, in the hills to the east. They are very different trips.

Ostia Antica: the easy one

From Piramide metro station, walk through to the Porta San Paolo terminus next door and take the suburban line towards the Lido, now signed Metromare. Ostia Antica is about half an hour down the line, and an ordinary Rome transport ticket covers the ride. From the station, cross the footbridge over the road and follow the signs for a few minutes.

The main street runs for more than a kilometre from the gate to the old shoreline. Along it, look for:

  • The theatre, first built under Augustus, where you can climb the seats.
  • The Square of the Corporations behind it: the offices of shipping firms, each with a mosaic on the floor showing its trade or its home port.
  • The Baths of Neptune, with a large black and white mosaic of the god and his sea horses, seen from a terrace.
  • A bar, the Thermopolium, with its marble counter and a painted picture of the food on offer.
  • Apartment blocks of brick, several storeys high, and bakeries with their lava millstones still in place.

Allow three hours. There is little shade and the paving is uneven, so bring water and proper shoes. The site has been closed on Mondays.

A floor mosaic in the Square of the Corporations at Ostia, where shipping firms had their offices. Photo: sailko, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.

Tivoli: three sights, and half a day is enough for one

Tivoli stands on a hill about thirty kilometres east of Rome, where the river Aniene drops out of the mountains. Regional trains run from Roma Tiburtina and take from forty-five minutes to more than an hour. Buses leave from Ponte Mammolo, on metro line B, and depend on the traffic.

Villa d'Este

Cardinal Ippolito d'Este, a son of Lucrezia Borgia, was made governor of Tivoli in 1550 after failing to become pope. He turned a hillside below his residence into a garden of fountains, all of them worked by the pressure of the river and not by pumps: the avenue of the Hundred Fountains, the Oval Fountain, and a fountain that plays an organ by water at set hours. It is in the town centre. Allow two hours, and expect a lot of steps.

The Hundred Fountains of Villa d'Este. Photo: Daderot, via Wikimedia Commons.

Hadrian's Villa

The emperor Hadrian built himself a country seat here in the second century, as large as a town: palaces, baths, libraries, a long pool lined with statues called the Canopus, and a round island retreat inside a moat. It is a ruin among olive trees, and a very large one. Allow two to three hours. It lies on the plain below Tivoli, several kilometres from the centre. A local bus links it with the town, and some buses from Rome stop within walking distance, so ask before you board.

The Canopus, the long pool of Hadrian's Villa. Photo: Livioandronico2013, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

Villa Gregoriana

This is a park and not a house. After a flood wrecked part of Tivoli in 1826, Pope Gregory XVI had the Aniene turned through tunnels in the hillside. The river now falls more than a hundred metres into the gorge beside the town, and paths wind down past caves and Roman remains to the foot of the waterfall and up again to two small temples on the edge of the cliff. Allow an hour and a half. The paths are steep, and the park has closed for part of the winter. It is the nearest of the three to the railway station.

The great waterfall of the Aniene, seen from the paths of Villa Gregoriana. Photo: Lalupa, via Wikimedia Commons.

Which one

  • You have a morning and no wish to plan: Ostia Antica. One train, one ticket, back in Rome for a late lunch.
  • You will not get to Pompeii: Ostia Antica. It is the nearest thing to it, without the crowds.
  • Gardens and water, or a hot day: Villa d'Este, with Villa Gregoriana if you have the legs.
  • Both villas of Tivoli: a full day, and by public transport a tiring one. A coach that links the two saves a good hour.
  • With small children: Ostia, where they can run in the theatre.

A third choice: Castel Gandolfo

The popes spent their summers above Lake Albano from the seventeenth century. In 2016 Pope Francis opened the palace as a museum. Trains from Roma Termini take about three quarters of an hour, and the town is a steep walk up from the station. The present pope has gone back to spending time at Castel Gandolfo, so check which rooms and gardens are open before you set out.

What the partner's tickets include

  • Ostia Antica Archaeological Park. Entry to the site and its museums. You exchange a voucher for a paper ticket at the ticket office. Transport is not included, and nor is a guide.
  • Villa Gregoriana. Entry to the park, by either gate. No guide.
  • Villa d'Este and Hadrian's Villa with a round trip from Rome. A coach from the edge of the Borghese gardens, near Flaminio metro station, with entry to both villas and some free time in Tivoli. The listing mentions a guide at the meeting point but does not list a guided visit, so read it before you count on one. This is a day out, not a half day.
  • Castel Gandolfo. Entry to the papal apartments and the Secret Garden. Getting there is up to you.

These are the tickets our partner sells for Ostia Antica, Tivoli and Castel Gandolfo, with today's prices:

[partner city="rome" match="ostia,gregoriana,este,hadrian,gandolfo" limit="4"]

Practical

State sites in Italy, these among them, have been free on the first Sunday of the month, and are busier for it. Hours for each place are on our pages for Ostia Antica, Villa d'Este and Hadrian's Villa.

From here

Beside the entrance to Ostia is a small walled village with a castle built in the 1480s for the future Pope Julius II, and places to eat. The beach at Lido di Ostia is a few stops further on the same train. In Tivoli, the old streets between Villa d'Este and the temples above the gorge are worth the walk. See what else there is in Tivoli and Rome, or open the map of Italy.

Cover photo: Rabax63, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

faqs.q: How do you get to Ostia Antica from Rome?
faqs.a: Take the suburban line towards the Lido from Porta San Paolo, beside Piramide metro station. Ostia Antica is about half an hour away, an ordinary Rome transport ticket is valid, and the site is a few minutes on foot from the station.

faqs.q: Is Ostia Antica worth visiting?
faqs.a: Yes. It is a whole Roman port town with a theatre, baths, mosaics, a bar and apartment blocks, half an hour from Rome and usually quiet. Allow three hours.

faqs.q: Can you see Villa d'Este and Hadrian's Villa in one day?
faqs.a: Yes, but it takes the whole day. They are several kilometres apart, so by public transport you need a local bus between them, or a coach trip that links the two.

faqs.q: How do you get to Tivoli from Rome by train?
faqs.a: Regional trains run from Roma Tiburtina to Tivoli in forty-five minutes to a little over an hour. Villa Gregoriana is the nearest sight to the station, and Villa d'Este is a walk through the town.

faqs.q: Is Ostia Antica better than Pompeii?
faqs.a: It is smaller and has no volcano, but it is far closer to Rome, much less crowded, and shows the working life of a Roman town very well. It is the better choice if you have only half a day.

title: Venice beyond San Marco: visiting La Fenice, and the smaller museums worth a ticket
subtitle: An opera house that burned twice, a designer's palace, dinosaurs on the Grand Canal, and lace and glass on the islands.

featured_image.alt: The auditorium of the La Fenice theatre in Venice seen from the stage: five gilded tiers of boxes under a painted blue ceiling

content_html:
[place attraction="la-fenice" city="venice"]

The company that built the opera house of Venice named it before a stone was laid. Their previous theatre had burned down, they had rebuilt it, and they had then lost it in a lawsuit. The new one, opened in 1792, was to be La Fenice, the phoenix, the bird that rises from its own ashes. The name turned out to be a forecast. The theatre burned in 1836 and was open again within a year.

On the night of 29 January 1996 it burned once more, down to the outer walls. Two electricians, whose firm was late with its work and faced a penalty, had set the fire. The city decided to rebuild the theatre as it was and where it was, from photographs, drawings and a film shot inside it, and La Fenice reopened in December 2003. You can see the result on any day without buying an opera ticket. It is a good start to a day in the Venice that lies away from San Marco.

Visiting La Fenice by day

The visit is on your own, with an audio guide, and takes about forty-five minutes. You see the foyer, the auditorium with its five gilded tiers, the royal box, first made for Napoleon, and the Apollonian rooms, the suite of halls used in the intervals. The front on Campo San Fantin and the entrance hall behind it are the parts that survived both fires.

This is the house where Verdi's Rigoletto and La traviata were first performed, in 1851 and 1853, the second to a poor reception. Rossini's Tancredi began here too, and in the twentieth century so did Stravinsky's The Rake's Progress.

The theatre is a working one. It closes to visitors, sometimes at short notice, for rehearsals and technical work, and on other days you may find the orchestra on stage while you look. Check the day before.

The front of La Fenice on Campo San Fantin. It survived both fires. Photo: Zairon, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

Palazzo Fortuny: a designer's house

Five minutes' walk from the theatre, on a small square, stands a large Gothic palace. Mariano Fortuny, born in Granada in 1871, took rooms in it at the end of the nineteenth century, then floor after floor, until the whole building was his workshop. He was a painter, a photographer, a stage designer who invented a lighting system for theatres, and the maker of the Delphos gown, a column of finely pleated silk that his clients kept rolled up in a hatbox.

The palace went to the city in 1956. Since 2022 it has been shown as his house: the long studio hung with his printed fabrics, his paintings, lamps and models, and his library. It suits anyone interested in textiles, fashion or theatre. Allow an hour.

Palazzo Fortuny, the Gothic palace that Mariano Fortuny turned into a workshop. Photo: Didier Descouens, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

The Natural History Museum

The building is the Fondaco dei Turchi, on the Grand Canal near the San Stae stop: a palace of the thirteenth century that served the Ottoman merchants of Venice as lodging and warehouse from 1621 to 1838, and was rebuilt very freely in the 1860s. Inside are the skeleton of an Ouranosaurus, a plant-eating dinosaur about seven metres long, brought back from the Sahara by a Venetian expedition in the 1970s, a giant fossil crocodile, the skeletons of two whales, and an aquarium that shows a rocky reef of the northern Adriatic. The rooms are well designed and dark, with little text. With children this is the best indoor hour in Venice.

The Fondaco dei Turchi on the Grand Canal, home of the Natural History Museum. Photo: Didier Descouens, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

Lace on Burano, glass on Murano

Both island museums are small, and each tells you about a craft that the shops outside sell in doubtful versions.

  • The Lace Museum is on the main square of Burano, in the school founded in 1872 to keep needle lace alive when only a few old women still knew the stitches. It shows lace from the sixteenth to the twentieth century, and on many days lacemakers work in one of the rooms. Half an hour. Burano is about forty-five minutes from Fondamente Nove on vaporetto line 12.
  • The Glass Museum is in a palace on Murano, the island to which the glass furnaces of Venice were moved by decree in 1291 because of the risk of fire. It goes from Roman glass to modern design. An hour. Murano is a short ride from Fondamente Nove.

The Lace Museum on the main square of Burano, in the former lace school. Photo: Abxbay, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.

Which one for whom

  • You love opera, or gilded rooms: La Fenice.
  • Textiles, fashion, photography: Palazzo Fortuny.
  • Travelling with children, or it is raining: the Natural History Museum.
  • You are going to the islands anyway: the two island museums. Do not cross the lagoon for the Lace Museum alone.

What the partner's tickets include

  • La Fenice Theatre ticket. Entry, with the theatre's audio guide to download to your own phone. Performances are not included. The listing says the ticket stays valid for a long period, so a sudden closure does not lose you the visit.
  • La Fenice ticket with audio tour. The same entry, with a tour in the partner's own app as well.
  • La Fenice sightseeing audio tour, without a ticket. The app tour alone. The title says it, and so do the exclusions: you buy entry yourself.
  • Palazzo Fortuny, the Natural History Museum, the Lace Museum. Plain entry tickets with no guide or audio guide.
  • Museums of Islands. One ticket for the Glass Museum and the Lace Museum. The boats are not included, and both museums stop admitting people in mid-afternoon, so start early.

These are the tickets and audio tours our partner sells for La Fenice and the smaller museums, with today's prices:

[partner city="venice" match="fenice,theatre,fortuny,merletto,natural,isole" limit="7"]

Practical

The four museums belong to the city's museum foundation. Each has its own weekly closing day, and they are not the same day, so check before you cross the lagoon. No ticket here includes the vaporetto. On some days of the year Venice has also charged day visitors an access fee, which is separate from all of this. Hours are on our pages for the Fortuny Museum, the Natural History Museum, the Lace Museum and the Murano Glass Museum.

From here

From La Fenice it is ten minutes on foot to the Accademia bridge, and less to San Marco. From Burano, a five-minute boat ride reaches Torcello and its cathedral with Byzantine mosaics. See what else there is in Venice and on Burano, or open the trip planner for Italy.

Cover photo: Pietro Tessarin, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

faqs.q: Can you visit La Fenice without seeing an opera?
faqs.a: Yes. The theatre is open for daytime visits with an audio guide on most days. It can close at short notice for rehearsals, so check the day before.

faqs.q: Is the La Fenice tour worth it?
faqs.a: Yes, if you like theatres or opera. In about forty-five minutes you see the auditorium, the royal box and the reception rooms of a house rebuilt exactly after the fire of 1996.

faqs.q: What can you do in Venice when it rains?
faqs.a: Visit La Fenice, Palazzo Fortuny or the Natural History Museum on the Grand Canal. All three are indoors and seldom crowded.

faqs.q: Is the Lace Museum in Burano worth it?
faqs.a: For half an hour, if you are on Burano already. It shows lace from the sixteenth to the twentieth century in the former lace school, and lacemakers often work there.

faqs.q: Which museum in Venice is best for children?
faqs.a: The Natural History Museum in the Fondaco dei Turchi, with a dinosaur skeleton, a giant fossil crocodile, whales and an aquarium.

subtitle: A day in the city itself, between the trips to Pompeii and Vesuvius: what to see above ground and below it.

featured_image.alt: The Alexander Mosaic from Pompeii: Alexander the Great on horseback charging at the Persian king Darius in his chariot, among spears and fallen soldiers

content_html:
[place attraction="national-archaeological-museum-naples" city="naples"]

In 1734 a prince of eighteen, Charles of Bourbon, took the throne of Naples. Through his mother, Elisabeth Farnese, the last of her line, he inherited one of the great art collections of Italy, gathered in Rome over two centuries by a family of popes and cardinals. Four years into his reign his engineers began digging at the foot of Vesuvius, first at Herculaneum and then at Pompeii, and statues, bronzes and painted walls started coming out of the ground by the cartload.

Both treasures ended up in one building. The Farnese marbles were shipped from Rome in the 1780s, and the finds from the buried towns were carried in from the royal palace at Portici. That building is the National Archaeological Museum, and it is the reason to give Naples a day of its own. Around it lies a city that still follows a Greek street plan, with as much underneath it as above.

The museum: what to look for

The building began in the 1580s as a cavalry barracks and later housed the university. Allow two to three hours.

  • The Farnese marbles, on the ground floor. The Hercules, over three metres tall, leaning tired on his club, and the Bull, a whole mountain scene cut from one block. Both were found in the 1540s in the Baths of Caracalla in Rome.
  • The mosaics from Pompeii, above all the Alexander Mosaic from the House of the Faun: Alexander charging at the Persian king Darius, in more than a million small stones. It has been under restoration since 2021, so ask whether it is on view.
  • The Secret Cabinet: the erotic paintings and objects from the buried towns, kept locked away for most of two centuries. Younger teenagers have needed an adult with them.
  • The wall paintings cut from the houses of Pompeii and Herculaneum.
  • The bronzes from the Villa of the Papyri at Herculaneum: two runners, a drunken satyr, a row of dancers with inlaid eyes.

Sections of this museum close and reopen all the time. The partner's listing itself names several that are shut, and says its ticket does not cover the Magna Graecia rooms. If you are going to Pompeii as well, it does not much matter which comes first: the site gives you the streets, and the museum gives you what was in the houses. The museum has been closed on Tuesdays.

The Farnese Hercules, more than three metres tall. Photo: patrick janicek, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0.

Underground: two small sites

The Ipogeo dei Cristallini

The Sanità district, north of the museum, lay outside the walls of the Greek city, and the Greeks buried their dead there. In 1889 a nobleman digging under his house in Via dei Cristallini broke into four tombs of the fourth and third centuries BC, cut into the soft yellow rock, with stone couches, painted garlands and a carved head of Medusa. They stayed private until 2022. Visits are by booked time in small groups, with a steep stair and no lift, and the listing says children under eight are not admitted.

A burial chamber of the Ipogeo dei Cristallini. Photo: MentNFG, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

The Lapis Museum

On Via dei Tribunali, under the church of Santa Maria Maggiore alla Pietrasanta, a lift goes down to the cisterns of the ancient aqueduct, which supplied the city's wells into the nineteenth century and sheltered its people from the air raids of the Second World War. The listing says visits are accompanied by staff, in Italian.

Neither of these is "Napoli Sotterranea", the best-known underground tour, which starts a few doors along the same street and which our partner does not sell.

Santa Maria Maggiore alla Pietrasanta. The Lapis Museum lies under it. Photo: Giuseppe Guida, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

A walk along the Greek streets

The Greeks who founded Neapolis in about 470 BC laid out three long parallel streets, crossed by narrow lanes. The plan is still there. The lower street is the one called Spaccanapoli, the Naples splitter, because from the hill above it looks like a cut through the roofs. A route of about two kilometres:

  • Piazza del Gesù Nuovo. A church with a front of pointed stone blocks, taken over from a palace of 1470. Free.
  • Santa Chiara. A plain Gothic church founded in 1310, burned out by bombs in August 1943 and rebuilt. The church is free. The cloister behind it, covered in painted tiles in the 1740s, has a ticket.
  • The Sansevero Chapel, a few steps off the street, with the Veiled Christ carved by Giuseppe Sanmartino in 1753. Ticket, by time slot, and it sells out. Our partner does not sell it.
  • Via San Gregorio Armeno, the lane of the workshops that make figures for nativity scenes, open all year.
  • The cathedral, where the blood of San Gennaro, the city's patron, is kept. Free.
  • Pio Monte della Misericordia, opposite, for one painting: Caravaggio's Seven Works of Mercy, of 1607. Ticket.
  • Via dei Tribunali, the middle street, back towards the museum: pizzerias, the Pietrasanta church and its brick bell tower.

Mind the scooters, and keep your phone and bag where you can feel them, as you would in any crowded street.

Via San Gregorio Armeno, the street of the nativity figure makers. Photo: Palickap, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

What the partner sells

  • The National Archaeological Museum entry ticket. Entry, with the temporary exhibition. The audio guide that comes with it is a general one about the city, not about the rooms.
  • Ipogeo dei Cristallini, standard entry. Entry with a virtual reality film, and an audio guide in English or Italian if you select it.
  • Lapis Museum. Entry, with no audio guide.
  • The "Cultural Legacy" audio tour. An hour's walk in the partner's app. Despite the name it covers the royal quarter, from Piazza Municipio to Castel dell'Ovo, and not the old centre.
  • The "Heart of Old Naples" audio walk. Longer: it starts in the royal quarter and ends among the old streets described above. No tickets are included.

These are the tickets and audio walks our partner sells for the old city of Naples, with today's prices:

[partner city="naples" match="archaeological,cristallini,lapis,legacy,heart" limit="5"]

A day in order

Start at the museum when it opens: the metro stops at its door. Walk north into the Sanità for the Ipogeo, come back for lunch on Via dei Tribunali, go down under the Pietrasanta, and finish with Spaccanapoli in the late afternoon, when the churches reopen after their midday break. Hours are on our pages for the National Archaeological Museum and the Ipogeo dei Cristallini.

From here

Further into the Sanità are the Catacombs of San Gennaro. South of the old centre, fifteen minutes on foot, the royal quarter begins: the San Carlo opera house, the Galleria Umberto I and Piazza del Plebiscito. See what else there is in Naples, or open the trip planner for Italy.

Cover photo: Lucas, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 2.0.

faqs.q: Is the Naples Archaeological Museum worth it?
faqs.a: Yes. It holds the best of what was found at Pompeii and Herculaneum, mosaics, wall paintings and bronzes, together with the Farnese marbles from Rome.

faqs.q: How long do you need at the Naples Archaeological Museum?
faqs.a: Two to three hours for the Farnese marbles, the mosaics, the Secret Cabinet, the wall paintings and the bronzes from Herculaneum.

faqs.q: Should you visit the Naples museum before or after Pompeii?
faqs.a: Either order works. The site shows you the streets and houses, and the museum shows you what was taken out of them.

faqs.q: What is the Ipogeo dei Cristallini?
faqs.a: Four painted Greek tombs of the fourth and third centuries BC, cut into the rock under a house in the Sanità district. They were found in 1889 and opened to visitors in 2022.

faqs.q: What is free to see in the old centre of Naples?
faqs.a: The streets themselves, the church of the Gesù Nuovo, the church of Santa Chiara, Via San Gregorio Armeno and the cathedral. The Santa Chiara cloister, the Sansevero Chapel and Pio Monte della Misericordia need tickets.
